newsitem.title: USA: FY98 farm spending bill boosts food safety funding.
newsitem.headline: FY98 farm spending bill boosts food safety funding.

text.p: The House Appropriations Committee subcommittee on agriculture today approved a $49.4 billion fiscal 1998 spending bill that provides increased funding for food safety and child nutrition programs.

The bill also caps USDA's main farm export subsidy program at $270 million--well below the Clinton administration's request of $500 million. However, that program has not been used in recent years due to favorable market conditions.

Overall, the spending bill provides $3.68 billion less for Agriculture Department and Food and Drug Administration programs than in fiscal 1997. It is also under $50 billion for the first time in recent memory.
In late January, President Clinton unveiled a food safety initiative aimed at reducing food-borne illnesses through increased surveillance, research and education.
The panel approved $43.2 million in funding for those activities, up $17.1 million from last year.
An additional $15.7 million was also provided for the agriculture department's meat and poultry inspection programs.
However, the panel ignored a Clinton administration request to fund $390 million of the inspection service's budget by imposing new users fees on meat-packing facilities.
Despite its request, the administration did not follow through on a promise to submit user fee legislation, Committee Chairman Joe Skeen, a New Mexico Republican, said.

The panel also rejected an administration request to increase user fees for grain inspection and chose not to fund the office of the USDA undersecretary for food safety, a position that has been vacant for some time.
The bill provides $3.92 billion for the Women, Infants and Children supplemental nutrition program, an increase of over $100 million from the current fiscal year.
However, overall funding for USDA Food, Nutrition and Consumer Services programs, such as food stamps, was reduced by more than $3.0 billion as a result of last year's welfare reform legislation.
Providing adequate money to pay crop insurance agent commissions posed a problem for the panel, Skeen said.
In recent years, those fees have been paid for out of the "mandatory" portion of the agricultural budget, which is the responsibility of the House Agriculture Committee.
However, the task of paying for those fees reverts back to the appropriations panel in fiscal 1998 under an arrangement that was worked out in 1994 crop insurance reform legislation.

After consultations with House Agriculture Committee Chairman Robert Smith, an Oregon Republican, Skeen said the panel decided to pay for agent fees in fiscal 1998 by capping EEP spending at $270 million.
That could pose a problem for USDA if U.S. wheat prices continue to slip and the European Union reactivates its own wheat export subsidy program at a more aggressive level than in recent years.
The spending bill provides just under $1 billion for the fiscal 1998 PL480 food aid program, down slightly from the current year.
The Market Access Program, which is used to promote U.S. agriculture products in foreign markets, is fully funded at $90 million.
The panel also approved full funding for the GSM-102 and -103 export credit programs, which help foreign nation finance purchases of U.S. agricultural goods.
The full House Appropriations Committee is scheduled to take up the spending bill on July 9. Once the House finishes its work, the Senate will move on the bill.
((By Doug Palmer, 202 898 8341))
